blocks.prompt: The King That Crunched Bones
blocks.text: T. rex was one of the biggest hunters that ever walked on land. It was as long as a school bus. Its head was longer than you are tall, and it had about sixty teeth. Each big tooth was shaped like a banana, thick and pointy. T. rex could bite so hard that it broke bone. Its arms were small next to the rest of it, but they were strong. It walked on two legs and held its long tail out straight behind it. T. rex lived a very long time ago. Now we dig up its bones and put them back together.

3.title: The King That Crunched Bones
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: Tyrannosaurus rex means tyrant lizard king
About forty feet from nose to tail
The skull is five feet long
The biggest tooth found is a foot long
It lived in western North America
Nobody knows what the arms were for

blocks.prompt: The Tyrant Lizard King
blocks.text: Its full name is Tyrannosaurus rex, which means tyrant lizard king. A tyrant is a ruler who takes whatever it wants. T. rex lived in the warm forests and river plains of western North America about sixty-six million years ago. From nose to tail it stretched about forty feet, longer than a school bus, and it weighed as much as a big elephant. The head did the work. A T. rex skull is five feet long and holds about sixty teeth. The biggest tooth ever found is a foot long, counting the root buried in the jaw. Most hunters have teeth like knives, made for slicing. T. rex had teeth like thick spikes, made for pressing down hard without snapping. It did not slice. It crushed. We know this because scientists have found fossil dung with smashed bone inside it. T. rex bit straight through bone and swallowed the pieces. Then there are the arms. Each one was about three feet long, roughly the length of a grown-up's arm, which sounds fine until you remember the rest of the animal was the size of a bus. They were thick with muscle, so they were good for something. Nobody has worked out what. That is one of the best things about dinosaurs. Even now, there are questions we cannot answer.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.
items: What does the name Tyrannosaurus rex mean?
How are T. rex teeth different from most hunters' teeth?
How do we know T. rex ate bone?
Why do you think scientists still argue about the arms?
answers: tyrant lizard king
they are thick spikes for crushing, not thin knives for slicing
fossil dung has been found with smashed bone inside it
(inference: the arms are strong but too short to reach the mouth, and fossils cannot show behavior)

4.title: The King That Crunched Bones
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Huge smell center in the brain
Eyes faced forward, like yours
Bite estimated near eight thousand pounds
Broken teeth were replaced for life
Built to walk far, not to sprint
Weighed six tons or more

blocks.prompt: How to Build a King
blocks.text: A T. rex skull is a toolbox, and every tool in it tells you something about how the animal lived. Start with the nose. The part of the brain that handled smell was enormous, larger in proportion than in almost any other dinosaur we know of. An animal that smells that well can find a meal from a long way off, alive or long dead, without ever seeing it. Now the eyes. Most hunted animals have eyes on the sides of the head so they can watch for danger in every direction at once. T. rex had eyes pointing forward, like yours. Two eyes aimed at the same object from slightly different angles give you depth. You can tell exactly how far away something is, which matters a great deal if you plan to close that distance. Then the jaw. T. rex teeth are not blades. They are thick, round-sided spikes with rough sawing edges, built to take enormous pressure instead of shattering. The skull bones were fused and braced to carry the load. Scientists estimate that load at around eight thousand pounds at the back teeth, the hardest bite ever measured for a land animal. And the teeth kept coming. When one broke off in a meal, a fresh one grew in behind it, over and over, for the whole of the animal's life. Last, the legs. T. rex had long shins and tightly packed foot bones, a design that usually belongs to animals built to cover ground steadily rather than to sprint. A six-ton body cannot afford to trip. None of this proves how T. rex hunted, or whether it hunted at all. It tells us what the animal was equipped to do. The rest is argument.

5.title: The King That Crunched Bones
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905
Sue, in Chicago, is about 90 percent complete
Teenage T. rex gained roughly four pounds a day
Sue died at about twenty-eight years old
Healed bite marks prove it attacked living animals
Probably walked near three miles an hour

blocks.prompt: The Argument About the King
blocks.text: For most of the twentieth century, T. rex was drawn as a monster: upright, tail dragging, roaring at the sky. Almost every part of that picture has since been thrown out, and the story of how it was thrown out is more interesting than the monster ever was. Take posture. The tail does not drag. A T. rex skeleton balances at the hip like a seesaw, body forward, tail counterweighted behind, and no fossil trackway has ever shown a tail groove. Take speed. Films sprint T. rex after a car at forty miles an hour. Computer models of its muscles and leg bones say otherwise: at a run, the forces would likely have shattered its own legs. Recent studies suggest a comfortable walking pace close to three miles an hour, which is roughly your pace on the way to the mailbox. Slow, but relentless. Then take the loudest argument of all. In the 1990s the paleontologist Jack Horner made a case that T. rex was mainly a scavenger, an eater of the already dead, pointing to the huge smell center in its brain and to arms too short to grapple with anything. The evidence answered him. Fossil hunters found an Edmontosaurus with T. rex tooth marks in its tail, and the bone around the wound had healed over. Healing requires a living animal. Something the size of a T. rex bit that dinosaur, and that dinosaur walked away. Growth studies added more. By measuring rings inside T. rex bones, the way you read rings in a tree, scientists found a violent teenage growth spurt: roughly four pounds a day, every day, for several years. Sue, the great skeleton in Chicago, is about ninety percent complete and shows an animal that lived to about twenty-eight. Almost none of this came from finding a bigger fossil. It came from asking better questions of the fossils already in the drawer. The monster shrank. The animal got stranger, and far more real.

6.title: The King That Crunched Bones
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Lived about 68 to 66 million years ago
Roughly 2.5 billion may have lived in total
About fifty good skeletons have been found
Skin patches found so far show scales
Its relative Yutyrannus had feathers
Birds are living dinosaurs

blocks.prompt: Reading the King: What a Fossil Can and Cannot Say
blocks.text: Tyrannosaurus rex is the most famous animal that no human has ever seen, and that sentence contains the whole problem. Everything we claim about it is an inference, built from stone copies of bones by people who arrived sixty-six million years too late. What makes T. rex worth studying is not that it was enormous. It is that it shows you exactly how far careful inference can be pushed, and precisely where it stops. Start with what the bones say plainly. The skull is five feet long, fused and buttressed to absorb force. The teeth are not blades but thick serrated spikes, and their arrangement, combined with jaw muscle reconstructions, yields an estimated bite near eight thousand pounds at the back teeth, the highest ever calculated for a land animal. Fossil dung containing pulverized bone confirms that the bite was used the way the anatomy suggests. The olfactory bulbs are proportionally vast. The eye sockets face forward, granting binocular overlap and true depth perception. That is not interpretation. That is measurement. Now watch inference do real work. Nobody watched a T. rex grow, yet we know how it grew. Cut a fossil bone across and it holds growth lines, like a tree. Plot the lines from many individuals of different sizes and a curve appears: a slow start, then an explosive adolescence adding roughly four pounds a day for several years, then a plateau. Sue, the Chicago skeleton, died at about twenty-eight. Inference reaches further still. In 2021, researchers combined body size, energy needs, and range to estimate that about twenty thousand adult T. rex were alive at any moment, that some two and a half billion lived across the species' existence, and that we have recovered around fifty decent skeletons from that number. Roughly one individual in every eighty million left a fossil we later found. The species we consider well understood is known from a statistical rounding error. And here is where inference stops. We do not know what the arms were for. They are three feet long, densely muscled, capable by one estimate of lifting several hundred pounds, and unable to reach the mouth. Every explanation offered, mating grip, pushing up off the ground, holding prey, remains an untested story. We do not know its color. We do not know whether it was feathered. Its close relative Yutyrannus wore a coat of filaments, and every skin patch recovered from T. rex itself so far is scaly, which settles nothing about the parts we have not found. We do not know the sound it made. The roar you are imagining was engineered by a sound designer from an elephant and an alligator. So the honest summary is this. We can weigh its bite to the pound and count the years of its life, and we cannot tell you its color, its voice, or the purpose of its own arms. That gap is not a failure of science. It is science being precise about the edge of its evidence, which is the one habit that separates it from a good story. The tyrant lizard king rules a kingdom of careful uncertainty, and he is more interesting there than he ever was in the movies.
